name: Aaron Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential; please tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company with a bachelor's degree. I maintain archive search software, fixing links between scanned pages and the names people search; I like when a family can find the correct record rather than a convincing wrong one. I don't use AI tools and prefer the archivist's reference index when names are close. My partner works as a physiotherapist, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a search tool may help find old files, but someone must check the original page before attaching a person's name. I do not use AI tools; I work from the scanned record and the archive's reference number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays limited, I expect my job to continue. I earn well for a mid-level developer, my partner is a physiotherapist with regular hours, we have about nine months of expenses saved, and plenty of software employers are nearby. The mortgage is affordable on our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the archive search screen and checking bad matches against the original scans. In the first year we'd add 200 to savings monthly while both wages hold, and I'd ask the archivist for the old index when a name looks wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I would enjoy fewer spelling corrections, provided we do not attach the wrong history to a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error did the original page catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A 1920s register had two people with the same surname and nearly the same first name. The scanned 1920s register separated two people with similar names, but our search result mixed their records until I corrected it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about old handwriting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children think the old handwriting looks like a puzzle. I tell them to look at the whole page before deciding what one word says.

I'd say **reference numbers** matter when names look alike.
think: I expect **my developer wage** to hold under modest AI change.
I have **nine months saved**, two regular wages and many nearby firms.
do: Keep fixing the **archive search screen** and checking original scans.
Ask the **archivist for old indexes** when a match seems wrong.
Save **200 monthly** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about household income, careful with family records.

fieldNote: **Nine months saved** and two regular wages support calm about the current job and mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could read records, write code and answer archive users, so our team should say which checks still need people. I will not call a result accurate just because it looks neat on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job could shrink if a smaller team uses AI to index pages and fix search code. I have savings and many local firms, but other employers may also trim this kind of work; I would be slower than colleagues who already use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing archive links while asking my manager to include the two-lookalike-name case in any archive AI trial. If a colleague who uses the tool walks me through it, I'd compare ten old search results with the pages; in the first year we'd hold off a planned study-room renovation until the firm says how many developers it needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though not without options. I know the archive's old pages. Management may stop paying for my knowledge of old archive pages once a machine reads them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would a wrong archive match hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong names could affect a family tracing relatives. I'd ask the archivist to count how many links the trial gets wrong, not just how fast it indexes pages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household work could wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The room works with an old desk. My partner and I can wait before paying builders while the software team is being counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches archive indexing and code before hands-on robots appear around 2031. A family still needs a way to challenge a wrong record link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect much of our software work could disappear, perhaps my post. Nine months saved and my partner's physiotherapy wage buy us time, but I cannot assume the many nearby firms will still be hiring archive developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd put my corrected search cases into a work record without private user names and ask two local archives whether paid records-technician posts exist. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only where the hours and combined wages cover mortgage and school costs; if no paid role meets that test, I'd keep looking and ask the lender about options before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I could afford a search for a while, but I expect the software work I know to lose its price quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would handling paper be secure after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A records technician handles original pages and checks indexes, and robots might take more physical handling around 2031. I'd ask whether the archives are hiring people for that work beyond a brief changeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about a job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children their school stays the same while we check actual offers. We would not move house because a website listed a job with no hours or wage.

I'd ask for a **record-correction route** for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives archives time to find out which old pages machines still mishandle. Robots follow around 2034, but thinking AI reaches our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn physical records care if an archivist supervises me, though I might lose my developer role first. I would not pay for a conservation certificate unless a real paid role needed it; five years let me check that before spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the archive lead for a two-hour supervised paper-index exercise on the lookalike names, only if my software manager releases paid time. I'd complete the free records-handling module and ask the archivist to check my correction log; I'd buy a certificate only if a real paid opening requires it and its cost fits beyond mortgage and school bills. If coding ends after 2031, I'd apply only to written paid openings whose combined wages cover those bills and whose hours fit school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the coding wage, but five years would let me see whether the paper work is real. I am not going to call a day watching an archivist a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the paper index?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the supervised exercise I'd learn how to match the numbered original pages to the paper index without disturbing a fragile register. I would not handle an original register until trained and authorised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner need to see in an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask for the paid hours in writing and whether the rota fits school pickup. If not, I'd stay with my software wage while looking elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives us time to keep old records readable and corrections traceable. Thinking AI reaches the code in 2036, with hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be earning in records care or another software team; I cannot know which. For the next few years our good wages and nine-month cushion feel secure, though I would keep asking whether original pages still need a paid human keeper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wrong-name case log and fix search problems as they appear. We'd save 200 monthly while both wages hold, and in the first year after 2036 I'd move only for a signed archive or software offer whose combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. I can keep a useful record of my work and wait for actual offers rather than sell our house on a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your correction log contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The log would show both lookalike names, the reference numbers and the page that settled the match, without anyone's search history. I want a future employer to see why the corrected archive link is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about archive work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child likes history and asks about archive work. I'd tell them to visit one and see the daily work, then look at training costs and paid openings before choosing a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because indexing and code could change before the archive can check the errors. Notice before cuts, paid records-care training and real openings with wages that cover our mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a wrong archive link is harmless because it is old. A family can build a story around the wrong person, and I would rather leave a blank search result than invent their relative.

headlineQuote: A family can build a story around the wrong person, and I would rather leave a blank search result than invent their relative.
portrait: Aaron, **43**, is an experienced archive-search developer with a bachelor's degree who checks scanned pages against reference numbers.
His **higher pay**, partner's physiotherapy wage, nine-month cushion and many local software firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He avoids AI and remembers **lookalike names** that the search system wrongly linked.
Steady disruption makes him **anxious** about indexing and code; 2028 AGI alarms him despite strong savings.
With more time, he tests **paid records-care work** through supervised observation and funded training before considering a move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove indexing and coding work before errors are checked or paid alternatives appear.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice before cuts**, funded records-care training and real mortgage-covering openings would help.
